idiom_name: Compose[A, B, C](f func(A) B, g func(B) C) func(A) C
implementation_notes: Since Go 1.18 type parameters let one helper cover every type triple (go.dev generics tutorial), which removes the per-signature wrapper functions that the pre-generics idiom needed. Go has no composition in the standard library, so this helper is the idiomatic replacement for the classic combinator; because Go does not allow variadic type parameters, longer chains nest the binary helper or use a small chain type, and the generic form is the default wherever the toolchain supports it.
pitfalls: Each function value is an indirect call the compiler cannot inline through, so a chain applied per element costs more than the steps written inline.
Generic Compose is binary: Go has no variadic type parameters, so longer chains nest calls or fall back to a []func(string) string slice that loses the static types.
A nil func value panics at call time rather than failing to compile; validate steps built from configuration before composing them.

variants.name: Explicit func-value wrappers (pre-generics)
variants.idiom_name: hand-written wrapper or per-signature compose helper
variants.implementation_notes: Before generics, the same chain is an explicit function literal - `normalizeThenHash := func(x string) string { return hash(normalize(x)) }` - or one helper per signature, and it remains readable for short chains and toolchains that must stay pre-1.18. Go's first-class function values and closures (go.dev codewalk) make this direct: no composition library or combinator is required. Choose it for one-step adaptation and legacy modules; choose the generic variant when several chains with different element types share the codebase.
pitfalls: One helper per concrete signature multiplies with every new type; a second chain over a different type gets a copy-pasted helper instead of a call.
Widening steps to interface{} or string to avoid helpers moves type errors from compile time to runtime type assertions.
